title: Hilbert's 10th Problem OQ-04: Simplest Undecidable Diophantine Equation
description: Formalizes the complexity boundaries for undecidable Diophantine equations. Proves: (1) 0-variable equations are trivially decidable; (2) 1-variable linear equations are decidable by divisibility (ax=b ↔ a|b); (3) undecidability is monotone in variable count. Axiomatizes the Jones-Matiyasevich upper bound (9 variables suffice) and the 9-variable undecidability result. Documents the open gap: minimum variables for undecidability is between 3 and 9.

overview.historicalContext: Hilbert's tenth problem appeared as the tenth of twenty-three problems David Hilbert posed in his 1900 address to the International Congress of Mathematicians in Paris: produce an algorithm that, given any polynomial equation in many unknowns with integer coefficients, decides whether it has an integer solution. The path to the negative answer took seventy years and four mathematicians. Martin Davis, Hilary Putnam, and Julia Robinson (1961) reduced the problem to the existence of a single Diophantine relation of exponential growth (the 'J-R hypothesis'); Yuri Matiyasevich (1970, in his PhD work in Leningrad) supplied that relation by encoding the Fibonacci numbers as a Diophantine condition, completing what is now called the MRDP theorem. The proof immediately raised quantitative questions: how many variables and how high a degree are needed in the resulting universal polynomial? Matiyasevich's first explicit construction used many dozens of variables; over the next decade he and others tightened the bound — Matiyasevich himself reaching 13 variables in 1977 — and James P. Jones (1982) gave the current record of 9 variables and degree 4, achieved simultaneously. On the lower-bound side, three variables are demonstrably necessary (one-variable polynomial decidability is classical, two-variable cases reduce to Pell-style methods). The gap between 3 and 9 variables, and between degrees 2 and 4, has not been narrowed in over forty years.
overview.problemStatement:
**The Open Question**: What is the simplest (fewest variables, lowest degree) Diophantine equation whose integer solvability is algorithmically undecidable?

Known bounds:
- Lower: degree ≥ 2 (degree-1 equations are decidable by Bézout/GCD)
- Lower: at least 3 variables needed
- Upper: degree ≤ 4, ≤ 9 variables suffice (Jones 1982)

The exact minimum remains open.
overview.proofStrategy: The file takes a survey approach, dividing the H10 complexity landscape into three classes and treating each according to its difficulty. (1) **Trivially decidable**: 0 variables — the polynomial reduces to its constant value, and `decide (P Fin.elim0 = 0)` is the algorithm; 1-variable linear — `linear_one_var` shows that `ax = b` has an integer solution iff `a ∣ b`, recovered by destructuring the existential. Both proofs are short and constructive. (2) **Provably undecidable, axiomatized**: 9-variable general — the MRDP theorem and its Jones-Matiyasevich quantitative refinement (9 variables, degree 4) are stated as axioms, and `nine_var_h10_undecidable` records the resulting undecidability of `H10_n_undecidable 9`. (3) **Bridging the two via a Lean-proved lemma**: `H10_undecidable_monotone` shows that `H10_n_undecidable n` implies `H10_n_undecidable (n+1)` by a many-one reduction. The reduction embeds an `n`-variable polynomial `P` as the `(n+1)`-variable polynomial `P̄(x) := P(x ∘ Fin.castSucc)` that ignores the last coordinate; one direction of the equivalence restricts a solution `y` of `P̄` to `y ∘ Fin.castSucc` for `P`, while the other extends a solution `x` of `P` by setting the last coordinate to 0 (the dependent if `if hlt : j.val < n then x ⟨j.val, hlt⟩ else 0` and a `convert ... using 2` step bridge the syntactic gap between `j.castSucc` and `⟨j.val, hlt⟩`). Iterating this lemma turns the single 9-variable axiom into undecidability for *all* `n ≥ 9` — the Lean-proved corollaries `ten_var_h10_undecidable` and `eleven_var_h10_undecidable` are samples of an infinite family. The capstone `complexity_gap_summary` packages 1-variable linear decidability and 9-variable undecidability into one theorem, locating the open boundary between them.
keyInsights: Degree-1 equations are decidable: $ax = b$ has a solution iff $a \mid b$ (classical Bézout); the multi-variable form $\sum a_i x_i = b$ has a solution iff $\gcd(a_1, \dots, a_n) \mid b$. This gives a hard lower bound: undecidability requires degree ≥ 2.

9 variables suffice for universality (Jones 1982): every r.e. set can be encoded by a 9-variable Diophantine equation. Combined with MRDP undecidability, this gives 9 as an upper bound on the variable count needed.

Undecidability is monotone: if $k$-variable H10 is undecidable, then $(k+1)$-variable H10 is also undecidable, via the embedding $P(x) \mapsto P(x \circ \text{Fin.castSucc})$ that ignores the last variable. By induction, this extends an axiom about a single $n_0$ to a theorem about every $n \ge n_0$.

The complexity gap: the undecidability threshold lies somewhere between degree 2 and degree 4, and between 3 and 9 variables. The exact bounds are unknown as of 2026 — no progress on the variable-count gap (3 vs 9) has been made in over forty years.

**Trade-off vs simultaneous optimum**: Jones (1982) achieved degree 4 *and* 9 variables jointly in a single universal polynomial; the joint optimum is not simply the pair (min variable count, min degree) achieved separately. Sharpening the joint bound is genuinely harder than sharpening either bound alone.

**Type-theoretic encoding choice**: decidability is stated as $\exists \text{alg} : \text{DiophantineN}\,n \to \text{Bool}$ rather than via the `Decidable` typeclass. This is deliberate: the `¬H10_n_decidable` form captures the algorithmic statement (no Turing machine decides solvability) without overcommitting to the much stronger statement that decidability fails inside the Lean type theory.
overview.text:
The question of 'simplest undecidable Diophantine equation' breaks into two sub-questions about degree and variable count.

**Variable count**: The 9-variable Jones (1982) result is the current best upper bound. Lower bounds come from algorithmic results for small variable counts (1-variable polynomial equations are decidable for bounded degree; 2-variable quadratic equations are often decidable by special methods).

**Degree**: Linear equations (degree 1) are decidable by Bézout's theorem. The degree-4 upper bound comes from Matiyasevich's encoding of Fibonacci numbers (and hence exponential growth) as degree-4 Diophantine conditions.

**Simultaneous optimization**: Jones (1982) showed that degree 4 and 9 variables can be achieved simultaneously — a single degree-4 polynomial in 9 unknowns is universal for all r.e. sets.

sections.mathContext: For each n, DiophantineN n = (Fin n → Int) → Int models n-variable polynomials. The decision problem H10_n asks for an algorithm that correctly decides solvability for all P : DiophantineN n.

sections.mathContext: A linear form a₁x₁ + ... + aₙxₙ + c = 0 is the degree-1 case. The decidability of all such equations is Bézout's theorem (axiomatized as linear_bezout_n).

sections.title: Proved Decidable Cases
sections.summary: Proves 0-variable decidability, 1-variable linear decidability (ax=b ↔ a|b), special cases, and H10_undecidable_monotone.
sections.mathContext: zero_var_decidable: 0-variable H10 checks a constant = 0. linear_one_var: ax = b has a solution iff a divides b (classical Bézout in 1 variable). H10_undecidable_monotone: an embedding Fin n → Fin (n+1) via castSucc shows undecidability propagates upward.

sections.title: Axioms from Literature
sections.mathContext: These axioms represent classical results: MRDP (1970), Jones-Matiyasevich 9-variable bound (1982), and the corresponding undecidability. linear_bezout_n is the general Bézout theorem for n-variable linear equations.

openQuestions.question: What is the minimum number of variables for an undecidable Diophantine problem?
openQuestions.notes: Known: at least 3, at most 9 (Jones 1982). Whether 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, or 8 variables are sufficient is unknown.

openQuestions.question: What is the minimum degree for undecidability?
openQuestions.notes: Degree ≤ 1 is decidable (proved). Degree 4 with 9 variables is undecidable. Whether degree 2 or 3 suffices for undecidability is unknown.

openQuestions.question: Can the Bézout axiom (linear_bezout_n) be proved in Lean 4 using Mathlib?
openQuestions.notes: Mathlib has Int.gcd and the extended Euclidean algorithm. A formal proof of the n-variable Bézout identity using Mathlib.Data.Int.GCD is feasible (~100 lines).

conclusion.summary: The file maps the complexity boundary of Hilbert's tenth problem with a four-part survey: (1) constructive decidability proofs for the trivial cases (0 variables, 1-variable linear); (2) a `LinearForm n` data structure for systematic study of degree-1 equations in any number of variables; (3) a clean monotonicity proof showing undecidability is upward-closed in variable count, via a `Fin.castSucc` reduction; and (4) five axioms from the literature (MRDP, Jones-Matiyasevich, 9-variable undecidability, n-variable Bézout, Jones universal polynomial). The `complexity_gap_summary` theorem packages the boundary into a single statement: degree-1 single-variable equations are decidable, 9-variable general equations are not — the open question lies strictly between.
conclusion.implications: Hilbert's tenth problem sits at the intersection of three foundational areas: number theory (Diophantine equations), computability (r.e. sets and reducibility), and proof theory (the MRDP encoding shows that elementary number theory is at least as expressive as recursion theory). The minimum-complexity question matters in several places. (i) **Lower bounds for proof complexity**: a small-variable, low-degree undecidable equation gives a minimal 'arithmetical encoding' of computation, useful in arithmetical hierarchy lower bounds and in the proof of Gödel's incompleteness via Diophantine encodings. (ii) **Number theory**: the simplest Diophantine equation whose solvability cannot be settled by any algorithm is presumably one whose solvability cannot be settled by any standard number-theoretic technique; sharper bounds would clarify which Diophantine techniques can in principle handle which complexity classes. (iii) **Computer algebra**: better lower bounds on undecidability would justify when computer-algebra systems are wasting effort on solvability questions, while better upper bounds (smaller universal polynomials) immediately give universal Turing machines of correspondingly small description. (iv) **Cryptography and post-quantum**: lattice-based and isogeny-based cryptosystems rest on hardness assumptions about specific Diophantine problems; understanding the boundary informs which families can support hardness assumptions.
openQuestions: **Variable-count gap (3 ≤ ? ≤ 9)**: Determine the minimum $n$ such that $\text{H10}_n$ is undecidable. The lower bound $n \ge 3$ is from algorithmic results for $\text{H10}_2$ (Pell-equation-style methods give decidability for many 2-variable cases, and conjecturally for all). The upper bound $n \le 9$ is Jones (1982). No progress in 40+ years.

**Degree gap (2 ≤ ? ≤ 4)**: Determine the minimum degree for an undecidable Diophantine family. Degree 1 is decidable (Bézout); degree 4 is undecidable (Jones). Whether degree 2 (quadratic Diophantine systems) or degree 3 (cubic) suffices is unresolved.

**Eliminate `linear_bezout_n` axiom**: Prove the n-variable Bézout characterization in Lean using Mathlib's `Int.gcd` and the extended Euclidean algorithm. Estimated ~100 lines; this would reduce the file's axiom count from 5 to 4 (oq-03 in the openQuestions list).

**Constructive Jones polynomial**: Replace `jones_universal_poly` with an explicit 9-variable degree-4 polynomial whose universality is mechanically verified. Jones (1982) gives an explicit construction; transcribing it into Lean would make the axiom into a definition + theorem (likely a multi-thousand-line undertaking but tractable).
